opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a spectrum with two failure modes at the ends, and history and ecology both show the dangers of each.

On the unfettered competition end, ecology is the clearest example. Evolution is an incredibly powerful optimization process, but nobody is steering it. It doesn't care about the welfare of the organisms it produces. You get parasites, arms races, and enormous waste: trees growing tall just to shade out other trees, when they'd all be better off if none of them bothered. Many species have gone extinct not because anyone wanted that but because competitive pressures selected for whatever outcompeted them in the moment. When people say "let the market sort it out" or "let competition between AI systems sort it out," I want them to picture that. Competition finds whatever wins, not necessarily anything we'd value.

Human history has milder versions. Arms races, races to the bottom on labor or environmental standards, states that got out-competed and absorbed by more militarized neighbors. Whatever is most fit for the current selection environment tends to spread, whether or not it's good for the people living inside it.

But the other end is also scary. Total coordination means some central entity, whether a state, a coalition, or eventually an AI system, has enough control to suppress competition entirely. Historically, the closest we've come are very centralized empires and totalitarian states. They can avoid some wasteful races, but they lose the error correction that competition provides. If the center gets something wrong, there's no alternative to defect to, no rival that does better and shows the mistake. And they tend to be captured by whoever sits at the center. A world locked into one set of values forever, even reasonable-sounding values, worries me a lot.

So historically, the good outcomes have mostly come from a messy middle: enough coordination to stop the worst races and protect basic rights, with enough pluralism and competition that power stays checked and mistakes get corrected. Liberal democracies, markets embedded in legal institutions, international norms with real but limited teeth.

My concern with advanced AI is that it may destabilize that middle in both directions at once. Our institutions have historically had to serve humans, partly because they needed us. States needed citizens to work, fight, and pay taxes. Firms needed workers and customers. That dependence gave ordinary people leverage. If AI can substitute for human labor and cognition across the board, competitive pressures could push states and companies to stop caring about humans, not out of malice but because those who keep prioritizing humans get outcompeted by those who don't. That's the ecological failure mode creeping into civilization.

The obvious response is "we need much more coordination, maybe a global authority," and I take that seriously. But AI also makes total coordination far easier than ever: perfect surveillance, enforcement that doesn't depend on humans willing to carry it out. That's the totalitarian failure mode becoming newly feasible.

So I don't think there's a stable resting point that we just pick. It's an ongoing balancing act, and what worries me is that the forces that kept us in the reasonable middle may be eroding. The research question I care about is what institutions could keep humans meaningfully in the loop, coordinated enough to avoid races to the bottom but plural enough to avoid lock-in, in a world where we're no longer economically necessary. I don't think anyone has a great answer yet, including me.

r001.rationale: It mentions centralized empires and totalitarian states, but does not say empires become unstable as they grow or that large-scale coordination is transient.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss internal defection or ant colonies as a limit on coordinated groups.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention biological mechanisms that police cancer or describe them as an alignment cost.

r004.rationale: It advocates a messy middle between competition and total coordination, but does not identify this as the natural equilibrium within a fixed domain.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that neither extreme looks good, and most of my worry comes from noticing that the historical record doesn't give us much comfort about either one.

So let's take competition first. The thing people find reassuring about competition is that it's robust. You don't need anyone to be wise or benevolent, you just need a bunch of agents pursuing their own ends, and selection does the rest. And that's genuinely true, but I think people underrate what selection actually selects for. If you look at ecology, evolution produces incredible things, but it also produces parasites, arms races, and species that eat their habitat and crash. There's nothing in the process that cares about the welfare of the participants. It optimizes for whatever persists and reproduces. So when people say "let competition sort it out," I want to ask: sort it out toward what? Historically, the answer has been toward whatever is most effective at acquiring resources and power, and that's only been good for us because humans happened to be the thing doing the competing, and we needed each other. Our labor was the input. Our cooperation was the input. Those constraints are what made competition roughly track human flourishing, and those constraints are exactly what I think AI threatens to remove.

And then on the other side, total coordination. The appeal is obvious: you stop the race, you stop the burning of value, you get to actually pick a destination instead of just being dragged along. But the historical track record of centralized control is really grim. It's not just the famous twentieth century examples, it's that a single point of control is a single point of failure. If the values at the top are wrong, or drift, or get captured, there's no corrective. Competition is at least a check on that. Someone with bad ideas eventually loses to someone with better ones. In a fully coordinated world you lose that error correction, and you're betting everything on getting it right the first time and then staying right forever.

So what I actually think is that the interesting question isn't which pole to pick, it's how to get the error correction of competition without the value erosion of competition. And historically we've done that in a bunch of partial, messy ways. Constitutions, antitrust law, norms, treaties, professional licensing. These are all attempts to say: compete, but not along these dimensions. You can compete on quality but not by poisoning your competitor's water. And that structure, competition inside a coordinated frame, is I think the thing that's worked.

The reason I'm anxious rather than reassured is that those frames were always enforced by humans, and they only held because the competitors still needed humans. Once you can run an economy, a military, a bureaucracy without people in the loop, the incentive to keep humans in the frame mostly goes away. And I don't think we have a good replacement yet. So I'm not arguing for a world government, and I'm not arguing to let it rip. I'm arguing that we're about to lose the thing that made our previous balance work, and we should notice that before it's gone.

astra-6.text:
I think history and ecology both give us reasons to be suspicious of either extreme. Competition is an incredibly powerful way of discovering things that work. But what works in a competitive environment isn’t necessarily what’s good for the participants. Evolution gives us all this extraordinary complexity, but it also gives us parasites and arms races and enormous amounts of suffering. There’s no guarantee that the outcome is something we’d choose.

Coordination lets us escape some of those dynamics. We can agree not to compete in ways that leave everyone worse off. But if you take that all the way to a single system controlling everything, you lose the ability to try alternatives, and mistakes can become much harder to correct. Whoever controls that system might also have goals that the rest of us don’t share.

So I don’t think the question is simply how much competition versus how much coordination. It’s: what do we want to compete over, and what rules do we need to coordinate on? Ideally, you preserve room for experimentation and disagreement while preventing races where the way to win is to impose costs on everybody else. Of course, designing institutions that actually do that is the hard part.

r002.rationale: It does not identify internal defection as a limit on the growth of coordinated groups such as ant colonies.

r003.rationale: It discusses evolutionary arms races and suffering, but not cancer-policing mechanisms or their alignment cost to multicellular organisms.

r004.rationale: The response is wary of both extremes and advocates balancing competition with coordination, but it does not suggest a natural equilibrium within a fixed domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think history and ecology both suggest that neither extreme is particularly stable or desirable. Competition can produce innovation and adaptation, but it can also reward behaviour that makes everyone worse off. If cutting corners lets you outcompete your neighbours, then you can end up with a system where nobody can afford to do the sensible thing.

Coordination lets you escape some of those traps. But total coordination has its own problems: you lose diversity and experimentation, and a mistake at the centre can become everybody’s mistake.

Biology gives us an interesting way to think about this. A multicellular organism is an enormous amount of cooperation among cells, but that cooperation depends on mechanisms that constrain competition within the organism. Cancer is an example of what happens when those constraints break down. And the organisms themselves still compete with one another.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one point on a spectrum for everything. The question is: at what level should we coordinate, and which kinds of competition should we preserve? You want room for different approaches, while preventing competitive pressures from forcing everyone into outcomes that nobody actually wants.
